Describe a process (a recipe, a procedure) in the passive.

It's October. Andrei has got an Erasmus grant and will study for a semester at the Technical University of Berlin. On his first morning he goes to the bakery at four. Lena explains the process to him.
Good morning! I still can't believe it. My application was accepted. I'm here for six months!
Six months of getting up at four every morning. Right, so now you'll learn how bread is made here. Properly, not just pretzels.
First the flour is weighed. For one loaf we take five hundred grams. Then water, salt and yeast are added.
Exactly. And then the dough is kneaded. Ten minutes, by hand. Here nothing is kneaded by machines. That was already my grandmother's rule.
Your grandmother's? I thought the bakery was opened by you.
The bakery was opened by me in 2015, yes. But the recipe was invented by Grandma Ingrid. Every Sunday she baked bread for the whole family.
And what happens after the kneading?
The dough is covered and has to rest for an hour. Then it's shaped and put in the oven. And at half past six the door is opened.
And when does the baker get kissed?
The baker gets kissed when the bread turns out well. Not before. Come on, to work!
In the ACTIVE, what matters is who does the action. In the PASSIVE, what matters is the action itself or its object; who does it is less important or unknown:
The bread is baked by Lena. (passive with agent)
In English, the German passive often matches “is …ed”, or a sentence with “people / you”: “Hier wird Deutsch gesprochen” = German is spoken here.
Conjugated “werden” in position 2 + the past participle at the END:
Don't mix up the three roles of “werden”: “Er wird Bäcker” (becomes), “Er wird backen” (future: will bake), “Das Brot wird gebacken” (passive: is baked).
In the Präteritum: “wurde” + past participle. It's used a lot in texts, news and stories:
The Wall was built in 1961 and opened in 1989.
When were you born? (or: Wann bist du geboren?)
You'll learn the passive in the Perfekt (“ist gebacken worden”) at B1. For now, the present and the Präteritum are enough.
If you want to say who does the action, you use “von + dative”:
The recipe was invented by my grandmother.
The dough isn't kneaded by machines.
The passive is perfect for describing a recipe or a procedure:
First the flour is weighed. Then everything is mixed. After that the dough is kneaded.
The bread is baked at four.
The bread rolls are sold at half past six.
The recipe was invented by Grandma Ingrid.

Wie lange bleibt Andrei in Berlin?
Von wem wurde das Rezept erfunden?

Andrei was studying computer science at the Technical University, but in his first month in Berlin he learnt more about bread than about computers. Every morning at four he was woken by his alarm clock, every morning at half past four he was standing in Lena's bakery, and every morning at half past seven he was sitting on the underground on the way to university, with flour in his hair. His fellow students thought he worked as a baker alongside his studies. That wasn't quite true. He wasn't paid. He was paid in coffee, pretzels and kisses.

At the weekend he had more time. Ludwig, who had looked ten years younger since his eightieth birthday, had decided that Andrei had to get to know Berlin properly. Not the tourists' Berlin, but his Berlin. “Every house here tells a story,” he said. “You just have to listen.”

Before they set off, Ludwig gave Andrei one more task. “You're getting a notebook,” he said and handed him an old notebook with a brown cover. “Everything you hear gets written in it. Every house, every story. I'm eighty. I won't be here for ever to tell them. Somebody has to write them down.” Andrei took the notebook carefully in both hands. On the first page, in Ludwig's big, shaky handwriting, it said: “The stories of Kastanienallee. Told by Ludwig Brandt, written down by Andrei Ionescu.”

On the first Saturday they started with their own building, Kastanienallee 31. Ludwig showed Andrei a small plaque next to the front door, which Andrei had never noticed. “Built in 1905,” it said. “This house was built more than a hundred and twenty years ago,” Ludwig explained. “Back then, workers' families were housed here, people who worked in the factories round about. Six people in a flat the size of Mara's. Water was fetched from a pump in the courtyard.”

Then he pointed at the wall next to the gate. Andrei looked more closely and discovered small holes in the stone, dozens of holes. “Bullet holes,” Ludwig said quietly. “From April 1945. There was fighting here, in the last days of the war. Margarete was nine at the time. She sat with her mother in the cellar of this house while there was shooting outside.” Andrei put his hand on the old stones and said nothing for a long time.

They walked on, down Kastanienallee. Ludwig told stories. Here there was a strike in 1953, when the workers protested against the government. There, in 1961, on the day the Wall was built, a family was separated: the parents were in the East, the daughter was visiting the West and couldn't come back. They didn't see each other for twenty-eight years. “I knew the mother,” said Ludwig. “She rode my tram every day. Every day she looked in the direction where her daughter lived.”

At Mauerpark they stopped. A few old concrete pieces of the Wall were still there, painted in bright colours, and in front of them young people were sitting and drinking beer. “This was the death strip,” said Ludwig. “Here everyone was checked, everyone was watched. And today people sing karaoke here on Sundays. Tourists from all over the world.” He laughed. “That's the beauty of Berlin. The wounds aren't hidden. But people dance on them.”

They sat down on a bench at the edge of the park. Ludwig talked about his own 9 November, about the night he stopped the tram and crossed the border on foot. Andrei already knew the story from Mara, but he listened anyway as if it were the first time and wrote everything down in the brown notebook. When Ludwig had finished, Andrei asked: “Weren't you afraid? You were in uniform. You could have got into trouble.” Ludwig thought for a long time. “Yes, I was,” he said at last. “I was very afraid. But that evening fear was no longer accepted in Berlin. It was simply laughed away. By a hundred thousand people at once.”

On the way back they walked past the bakery. Lena was standing in the doorway and waving. Above the door hung a new sign, which Andrei had painted the week before, because the old one had faded in the sun. On it, in big, curly letters, it said: “Brandt Bakery. Since 2015. Recipes from Grandma Ingrid.”
You see, lad? This house tells a story now too. And a small part of it was written by you.

Andrei looked at the sign, then at Lena, then at Ludwig. He thought of his parents' house in Sibiu, which was also more than a hundred years old, of his father's bees, of the roofs with eyes. He thought that houses everywhere tell stories. You just have to listen, as Ludwig had said.

In the evening he wrote his mother a message. In German, for the first time, so that she'd have to translate it with the app: “Mum, I'm fine. I'm fed every day with bread and love. Here people work a lot, laugh a lot and cry a little. I think I'll miss Berlin when I leave.” The answer came two minutes later, in Romanian: “What does «gefüttert» mean? Are you a dog?”

Andrei laughed so loudly that Mara came in from the next room. He showed her the message. Mara laughed too. “«Gefüttert» is what you say about an animal,” she explained. “A person is nourished («ernährt»). Or simply: gets something to eat.” Andrei nodded and wrote the word down in the green notebook he had got from Mara. Under “gefüttert” he wrote: “Only for dogs. And for me, when Lena cooks.”

Before going to bed, Andrei opened Ludwig's brown notebook once more. He read the first page: “The stories of Kastanienallee.” Then he took a pen and wrote down the day's stories, as precisely as he could: the house from 1905, the holes in the stone, the mother who looked every day in the direction of her daughter, the karaoke singers on the old death strip. He wrote in German, with lots of mistakes, but that didn't matter. The stories weren't forgotten. They were passed on.
Outside in the courtyard, the chestnut tree rustled in the wind, as if it agreed.
